opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to start by being clear about what we mean, because there's a lot of hype. When people hear "robotic surgery," they often imagine a robot autonomously performing an entire operation, and that's not what's happening and frankly not what I think is going to happen anytime soon. Most surgical robots today, like the da Vinci system, are really teleoperated. The surgeon is sitting at a console controlling every motion. The robot is an extension of their hands.

What I find exciting is partial autonomy, or what I sometimes call "augmented dexterity." The idea is that the surgeon remains in charge, but certain subtasks, ones that are tedious, repetitive, and well-defined, could be handed off to the robot. Think of suturing, for example. Closing up an incision can take a long time, and it's fatiguing. If the robot could take over that portion under the surgeon's supervision, the surgeon could focus their attention on the parts of the procedure that really require judgment and expertise.

It's a lot like what's happened with cars. We don't have fully self-driving cars everywhere, but we do have lane-keeping and adaptive cruise control, which make driving less exhausting and arguably safer. The driver is still responsible. I think surgery will follow a similar path.

The benefits are several. One is reducing surgeon fatigue, which is a real issue: these procedures can go on for hours, and fatigue leads to errors. Another is consistency. A robot can place sutures with very uniform spacing and tension, which may help healing. And then there's access. There are huge parts of the world, and even rural areas in the U.S., where there just aren't enough skilled surgeons. If we can make some of these subtasks more automated, a less specialized surgeon, or one supervising remotely, might be able to deliver higher-quality care to more people.

But I want to emphasize humility here. Surgery is extraordinarily complex. Tissue is soft, it deforms, it bleeds, every patient's anatomy is different. These are exactly the conditions where robots struggle. So I think progress will be incremental, task by task, with lots of careful validation. And I think that's the right way to do it. The goal isn't to replace surgeons; it's to give them better tools.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls partial autonomy “augmented dexterity” and describes robots taking over subtasks under the surgeon’s supervision, enhancing the surgeon’s capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I'm pretty skeptical of the idea that we're going to have fully autonomous surgical robots anytime soon. The human body is incredibly variable, tissue is deformable, there's bleeding, there's fluids, and the stakes are obviously very high. So I don't think the goal should be to replace the surgeon. The goal should be to augment the surgeon.

And that's where partial autonomy comes in. If you look at a long procedure, say a four or five hour operation, there are a lot of subtasks that are tedious and repetitive. Suturing is the classic example. Tying knots, closing an incision, debridement, which is removing dead tissue, or even just holding the camera steady and keeping it pointed at the right spot. These are things that surgeons do over and over, and they get fatigued. Fatigue leads to errors. So if a robot could take over some of those subtasks under supervision, the surgeon can step back, rest their hands, and focus on the parts of the procedure that really require judgment and expertise.

The analogy I like is a bit like autopilot in aviation. The pilot is still in the cockpit, still responsible, still monitoring everything. But for the long stretches of routine flying, the automation handles it, and the pilot's attention is reserved for takeoff, landing, and anything unexpected. That model has made flying dramatically safer, and I think something similar could happen in the operating room.

The other benefit, which I think people underappreciate, is access. There's a global shortage of surgeons, and in many parts of the world people simply don't have access to surgical care at all. If we can make surgeons more efficient, if one surgeon can supervise more procedures, or if certain routine steps can be done more consistently, that could expand access in a meaningful way.

Now, I want to be clear that we're still in early days here. In my lab at Berkeley we've been working on things like autonomous suturing and debridement for over a decade, and it's humbling. Things that look simple, like picking up a needle and passing it through tissue, turn out to be really hard for a robot. But the progress, especially with learning from demonstration and better perception, has been encouraging. So I'm optimistic, but it's a cautious optimism, and I think the human has to stay in the loop for a long time to come.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots taking over repetitive subtasks so surgeons can rest and focus on tasks requiring judgment, but it does not identify enhanced surgeon dexterity as a benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to assist surgeons by automating particular parts of a procedure. The surgeon is still in charge, making the clinical decisions, but the robot might handle a repetitive task like placing sutures, with the surgeon supervising and able to intervene.

That could reduce fatigue and help surgeons perform more consistently. And if we can reduce the time that procedures take without compromising safety, we could potentially make surgical care more accessible.

The key is knowing when the robot should ask for help. Surgery involves uncertainty: tissue moves, anatomy varies, and something unexpected can happen. So partial autonomy means developing systems that can recognize their limits and hand control back to the surgeon. I see that collaboration as a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes automating repetitive tasks, reducing fatigue, and improving consistency, but does not identify enhanced surgeon dexterity as a potential benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to help surgeons with particular parts of a procedure. Surgery involves an enormous amount of judgment, and you want the surgeon making those decisions. But there are subtasks—suturing, for example—where a robot could provide assistance, with the surgeon supervising and able to take over.

If we can make that assistance reliable, it could reduce fatigue and help surgeons work more consistently. Eventually, it might also make high-quality surgical care more widely available. But those are benefits we have to demonstrate. The key is knowing when the robot can act safely and when it needs to ask for help.

r001.rationale: The response describes assistance with subtasks such as suturing, reduced fatigue, and more consistent work, but does not identify enhanced surgeon dexterity as a potential benefit.
